claim: Protein kinase D (PKD) is a family of serine/threonine kinases required for the structural integrity and function of the Golgi complex.
source: Protein kinase D (PKD) is a family of serine/threonine kinases that is required for the structural integrity and function of the Golgi complex.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about PKD function.

claim: A Rho signaling network comprising GEF-H1, the RhoGAP DLC3, and the Rho effector PLCε regulates the activation of PKD at trans-Golgi membranes.
source: Using the genetically encoded PKD activity reporter G-PKDrep we now uncover a Rho signaling network comprising GEF-H1, the RhoGAP DLC3, and the Rho effector PLCε that regulate the activation of PKD at trans-Golgi membranes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data using the G-PKDrep reporter.

claim: The GEF-H1/Rho/PLCε/PKD molecular network coordinates the formation of TGN-derived Rab6-positive transport carriers delivering cargo for localized exocytosis at focal adhesions.
source: We further show that this molecular network coordinates the formation of TGN-derived Rab6-positive transport carriers delivering cargo for localized exocytosis at focal adhesions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data on Rab6 vesicle trafficking.

claim: The Golgi apparatus is the central sorting and modification station of transmembrane and secretory proteins and has a perinuclear localization in interphase mammalian cells.
source: The Golgi apparatus is the central sorting and modification station of transmembrane and secretory proteins and has a perinuclear localization in interphase mammalian cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Golgi apparatus function and localization.

claim: The integrity and position of the Golgi complex are primarily governed by the microtubule network, with a smaller contribution of the actin cytoskeleton.
source: The integrity and position of the Golgi complex are primarily governed by the microtubule network, with a smaller contribution of the actin cytoskeleton (Allan et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by Allan et al., 2002.

claim: Microtubules are implicated in the transport of vesicles from the Golgi and localized exocytosis.
source: Microtubules are also implicated in the transport of vesicles from the Golgi and localized exocytosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about microtubule function in vesicular transport.

claim: During directed migration of cells, microtubule remodeling positions the Golgi complex towards the leading edge to support polarized transport.
source: Furthermore, during directed migration of cells, microtubule remodeling positions the Golgi complex towards the leading edge to support polarized transport and is further required for the rapid turnover of focal adhesions (FAs) (reviewed in [Kaverina and Straube, 2011]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Kaverina and Straube, 2011.

claim: Microtubule remodeling is required for the rapid turnover of focal adhesions.
source: Furthermore, during directed migration of cells, microtubule remodeling positions the Golgi complex towards the leading edge to support polarized transport and is further required for the rapid turnover of focal adhesions (FAs) (reviewed in [Kaverina and Straube, 2011]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Kaverina and Straube, 2011.

claim: The crosstalk between microtubules and the Golgi complex is coordinated by signaling factors including small GTPases such as Cdc42, Arf1, and Rho and their respective GEF and GAP proteins.
source: The crosstalk between microtubules and the Golgi complex is coordinated by signaling factors including small GTPases such as Cdc42, Arf1, and Rho and their respective GEF and GAP proteins (reviewed in [Millarte and Farhan, 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Millarte and Farhan, 2012.

claim: Arf1-mediated recruitment of the Cdc42-specific GAP ARHGAP21 (ARHGAP10) to Golgi membranes controls Cdc42 activity and microtubule-dependent positioning of the Golgi complex.
source: For example, Arf1-mediated recruitment of the Cdc42-specific GAP ARHGAP21 (ARHGAP10) to Golgi membranes controls Cdc42 activity and microtubule-dependent positioning of the Golgi complex (Dubois et al., 2005; Hehnly et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dubois et al., 2005 and Hehnly et al., 2010.

claim: Rho hyperactivation leads to Golgi complex fragmentation.
source: Although Rho hyperactivation has been reported to lead to Golgi complex fragmentation (Zilberman et al., 2011), the physiological relevance of this observation is not clear.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zilberman et al., 2011.

claim: ARHGEF2/GEF-H1 is a RhoGEF that is sequestered by microtubules.
source: ARHGEF2/GEF-H1 is a RhoGEF that is sequestered by microtubules and it is further regulated downstream of G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) ligands (Meiri et al., 2009, 2014) and ERK signaling (Guilluy et al., 2011; Kakiashvili et al., 2009; Scott et al., 2016; Waheed et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: GEF-H1 is regulated downstream of G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) ligands.
source: ARHGEF2/GEF-H1 is a RhoGEF that is sequestered by microtubules and it is further regulated downstream of G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) ligands (Meiri et al., 2009, 2014) and ERK signaling (Guilluy et al., 2011; Kakiashvili et al., 2009; Scott et al., 2016; Waheed et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Meiri et al., 2009, 2014.

claim: GEF-H1 is regulated downstream of ERK signaling.
source: ARHGEF2/GEF-H1 is a RhoGEF that is sequestered by microtubules and it is further regulated downstream of G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) ligands (Meiri et al., 2009, 2014) and ERK signaling (Guilluy et al., 2011; Kakiashvili et al., 2009; Scott et al., 2016; Waheed et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guilluy et al., 2011; Kakiashvili et al., 2009; Scott et al., 2016; Waheed et al., 2010.

claim: GEF-H1 has been involved in exocytosis at the plasma membrane, FA turnover, response to mechanical forces, cell migration, and cell polarity.
source: GEF-H1 has been involved in exocytosis at the plasma membrane, FA turnover, response to mechanical forces, cell migration, and cell polarity (reviewed in [Pathak and Dermardirossian, 2013]), however, so far it has not been connected to vesicle fission at the Golgi complex.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Pathak and Dermardirossian, 2013.

claim: GEF-H1 has not been connected to vesicle fission at the Golgi complex prior to this study.
source: GEF-H1 has been involved in exocytosis at the plasma membrane, FA turnover, response to mechanical forces, cell migration, and cell polarity (reviewed in [Pathak and Dermardirossian, 2013]), however, so far it has not been connected to vesicle fission at the Golgi complex.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The protein kinase D (PKD) family of serine/threonine kinases consists of PKD1, PKD2, and PKD3 in mammals.
source: The protein kinase D (PKD) family of serine/threonine kinases consisting of PKD1, PKD2, and PKD3 in mammals is enriched at the trans-Golgi network (TGN) where it coordinates the fission of vesicles destined for the plasma membrane (Liljedahl et al., 2001; Malhotra and Campelo, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the PKD family composition.

claim: PKD is enriched at the trans-Golgi network (TGN) where it coordinates the fission of vesicles destined for the plasma membrane.
source: The protein kinase D (PKD) family of serine/threonine kinases consisting of PKD1, PKD2, and PKD3 in mammals is enriched at the trans-Golgi network (TGN) where it coordinates the fission of vesicles destined for the plasma membrane (Liljedahl et al., 2001; Malhotra and Campelo, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liljedahl et al., 2001 and Malhotra and Campelo, 2011.

claim: PKD is recruited to and activated at the TGN by the interaction with diacylglycerol (DAG) and Arf1.
source: PKD is recruited to and activated at the TGN by the interaction with diacylglycerol (DAG) and Arf1 (Baron and Malhotra, 2002; Pusapati et al., 2010) and through direct phosphorylation by PKCη (Díaz Añel and Malhotra, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baron and Malhotra, 2002 and Pusapati et al., 2010.

claim: PKD is activated at the TGN through direct phosphorylation by PKCη.
source: PKD is recruited to and activated at the TGN by the interaction with diacylglycerol (DAG) and Arf1 (Baron and Malhotra, 2002; Pusapati et al., 2010) and through direct phosphorylation by PKCη (Díaz Añel and Malhotra, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Díaz Añel and Malhotra, 2005.

claim: The level of DAG in TGN membranes controls the localization and activity of PKD.
source: Because the level of DAG in TGN membranes controls the localization and activity of PKD, the pathways contributing to the local production of DAG are critical regulators of PKD-dependent transport carrier formation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PKD regulation.

claim: PKD phosphorylates and activates the lipid kinase PI4KIIIβ thereby increasing PtdIns(4)P levels at the TGN.
source: For example, PKD phosphorylates and activates the lipid kinase PI4KIIIβ thereby increasing PtdIns(4)P levels at the TGN (Hausser et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hausser et al., 2005.

claim: Increased PtdIns(4)P levels at the TGN recruit the ceramide transfer protein CERT from the ER to the Golgi membranes.
source: This, in turn, recruits the ceramide transfer protein CERT from the ER to the Golgi membranes, where CERT contributes to PKD activation by providing ceramide as a precursor for further DAG production (Fugmann et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fugmann et al., 2007.

claim: CERT contributes to PKD activation by providing ceramide as a precursor for further DAG production.
source: This, in turn, recruits the ceramide transfer protein CERT from the ER to the Golgi membranes, where CERT contributes to PKD activation by providing ceramide as a precursor for further DAG production (Fugmann et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fugmann et al., 2007.

claim: The family of PI-PLC enzymes generate DAG and inositol trisphosphate (IP3) through the hydrolysis of PtdIns(4,5)P2.
source: Additionally, the family of PI-PLC enzymes, which generate DAG and inositol trisphosphate (IP3) through the hydrolysis of PtdIns(4,5)P2, are implicated in PKD activation downstream of Gβγ subunits (Bard and Malhotra, 2006; Díaz Añel, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PI-PLC enzyme function.

claim: PI-PLC enzymes are implicated in PKD activation downstream of Gβγ subunits.
source: Additionally, the family of PI-PLC enzymes, which generate DAG and inositol trisphosphate (IP3) through the hydrolysis of PtdIns(4,5)P2, are implicated in PKD activation downstream of Gβγ subunits (Bard and Malhotra, 2006; Díaz Añel, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bard and Malhotra, 2006 and Díaz Añel, 2007.

claim: Golgi-localized PKD activity is enhanced by drug-induced microtubule depolymerization.
source: We previously reported that Golgi-localized PKD activity is enhanced by drug-induced microtubule depolymerization (Fuchs et al., 2009) but how the microtubule network signaled to the TGN remained elusive.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work, Fuchs et al., 2009.

claim: GEF-H1 mediates PKD activation at the TGN upon nocodazole-induced release from microtubules.
source: Here, we identify GEF-H1 to mediate PKD activation at the TGN upon nocodazole-induced release from microtubules.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: GEF-H1 signals through RhoA and PLCε to control steady state and GPCR-induced activity of PKD at the TGN membranes.
source: We provide evidence that GEF-H1 signals through RhoA and PLCε to control steady state and also G-Protein coupled receptor (GPCR)-induced activity of PKD at the TGN membranes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: At the TGN, PKD activated downstream of Rho stimulates the fission of Rab6-positive exocytic carriers delivering cargo to FAs.
source: Most importantly, we show that at the TGN, PKD activated downstream of Rho stimulates the fission of Rab6-positive exocytic carriers delivering cargo to FAs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Through GEF-H1, the microtubule network controls anterograde trafficking from the TGN.
source: Consequently, through GEF-H1, the microtubule network controls anterograde trafficking from the TGN.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Nocodazole is a strong activator of PKD at TGN membranes.
source: Nocodazole is a strong activator of PKD at TGN membranes (Fuchs et al., 2009), suggesting that the microtubule network not only plays a structural role in maintaining Golgi complex position and shape but also signals to the Golgi complex to coordinate its function.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fuchs et al., 2009.

claim: Microtubule disruption releases the microtubule-associated RhoGEF GEF-H1 leading to the activation of the Rho GTPases RhoA and RhoB.
source: Microtubule disruption was described to release the microtubule-associated RhoGEF GEF-H1 leading to the activation of the Rho GTPases RhoA and RhoB (Arnette et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arnette et al., 2016 and Chang et al., 2008.

claim: Expression of constitutive active RhoA Q63L significantly increases PKD activity at the TGN up to twofold.
source: When cells expressed constitutive active RhoA Q63L, the reporter phosphorylation and thus PKD activity significantly increased up to twofold (0.2284 (median control)) versus 0.4826 (median RhoA Q63L)) whereas expression of wild type (wt) RhoA had no effect compared to the control cells (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B using the G-PKDrep reporter.

claim: Expression of wild type RhoA has no effect on PKD activity compared to control cells.
source: When cells expressed constitutive active RhoA Q63L, the reporter phosphorylation and thus PKD activity significantly increased up to twofold (0.2284 (median control)) versus 0.4826 (median RhoA Q63L)) whereas expression of wild type (wt) RhoA had no effect compared to the control cells (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Expression of RhoA Q63L results in Golgi fragmentation.
source: As reported previously, expression of RhoA Q63L resulted in Golgi fragmentation (Zilberman et al., 2011) and stress fiber formation (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zilberman et al., 2011 and experimental data shown in Figure 1A and C.

claim: Expression of RhoA Q63L results in stress fiber formation.
source: As reported previously, expression of RhoA Q63L resulted in Golgi fragmentation (Zilberman et al., 2011) and stress fiber formation (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and C.

claim: GFP-tagged RhoA Q63L localizes to TGN membranes indicated by co-localization with the trans-Golgi marker p230.
source: In support of a local role for RhoA in the activation of PKD we could detect GFP-tagged RhoA Q63L at TGN membranes indicated by the co-localization with the trans-Golgi marker p230 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Active RhoB Q63L localizes to the TGN and activates PKD at this site.
source: Similarly, active RhoB Q63L localized to the TGN and activated PKD at this site (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The co-localization of constitutive active RhoA and RhoB with Rab6 is significantly higher when compared to their wild-type counterparts.
source: Indeed, the co-localization of constitutive active RhoA and RhoB with Rab6 was significantly higher when compared to their wild-type counterparts, further supporting a role for active Rho at TGN membranes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D using Manders' coefficient analysis.

claim: GEF-H1 directly binds to microtubules and, when bound, is inactive.
source: GEF-H1 directly binds to microtubules and, when bound, is inactive (Krendel et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Krendel et al., 2002.

claim: With increasing microtubule depolymerization, GEF-H1 is released and free to activate Rho.
source: With increasing microtubule depolymerization, GEF-H1 is released and free to activate Rho (Arnette et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arnette et al., 2016 and Chang et al., 2008.

claim: In GEF-H1-depleted cells, nocodazole-induced PKD activation is strongly reduced.
source: Indeed, in GEF-H1-depleted cells nocodazole-induced PKD activation was strongly reduced (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: GEF-H1 can be activated downstream of ERK signaling.
source: GEF-H1 can be activated downstream of ERK signaling (Fujishiro et al., 2008; Guilluy et al., 2011; Kakiashvili et al., 2009; Waheed et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fujishiro et al., 2008; Guilluy et al., 2011; Kakiashvili et al., 2009; Waheed et al., 2010.

claim: In HEK293T cells, nocodazole treatment strongly induces the MAPK pathway.
source: In HEK293T cells, nocodazole treatment strongly induced the MAPK pathway.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: Simultaneous MEK1/2 inhibition does not impair phosphorylation of PKD, proving that GEF-H1-mediated PKD activation is independent of ERK.
source: Simultaneous MEK1/2 inhibition, however, did not impair phosphorylation of PKD (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) proving that GEF-H1-mediated PKD activation is independent of ERK.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Expression of GEF-H1 wt and GEF-H1 C53R is sufficient to activate PKD.
source: In agreement with our GEF-H1 depletion results, expression of GEF-H1 wt and GEF-H1 C53R, a mutant that does not bind microtubules and is thus constitutively active (Krendel et al., 2002), was sufficient to activate PKD (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and citation to Krendel et al., 2002.

claim: GEF-H1 C53R is a mutant that does not bind microtubules and is thus constitutively active.
source: In agreement with our GEF-H1 depletion results, expression of GEF-H1 wt and GEF-H1 C53R, a mutant that does not bind microtubules and is thus constitutively active (Krendel et al., 2002), was sufficient to activate PKD (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Krendel et al., 2002.

claim: GEF-H1 C53R induces stronger PKD activation compared to GEF-H1 wt.
source: Of note, GEF-H1 C53R induced PKD activation was stronger compared to GEF-H1 wt.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Expression of GEF-H1 C53R induces fragmentation of the Golgi complex.
source: Analogous to the expression of active RhoA, expression of GEF-H1 C53R induced fragmentation of the Golgi complex whereas in cells expressing GEF-H1 wt the Golgi complex remained compact (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In cells expressing GEF-H1 wt, the Golgi complex remains compact.
source: Analogous to the expression of active RhoA, expression of GEF-H1 C53R induced fragmentation of the Golgi complex whereas in cells expressing GEF-H1 wt the Golgi complex remained compact (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In cells expressing GEF-H1 wt, G-PKDrep phosphorylation is significantly enhanced compared to control cells without ectopic GEF-H1 expression.
source: In cells expressing GEF-H1 wt, the reporter phosphorylation was significantly enhanced compared to the control cells without ectopic GEF-H1 expression (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: G-PKDrep phosphorylation is stronger in the case of GEF-H1 C53R expression compared to GEF-H1 wt.
source: In agreement with the quantitative Western Blot results (Figure 2B), reporter phosphorylation was stronger in the case of GEF-H1 C53R expression (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The RhoA biosensor displays partial co-localization with a co-expressed Golgi marker protein (mRuby-Golgi-7) in HeLa cells.
source: This RhoA biosensor was described to co-localize with Golgi membrane markers (Pertz et al., 2006). In HeLa cells the RhoA biosensor also displayed a partial co-localization with a co-expressed Golgi marker protein (mRuby-Golgi-7) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and citation to Pertz et al., 2006.

claim: Nocodazole stimulation leads to a GEF-H1-dependent increase in RhoA activity in the cell periphery.
source: As previously reported (Reinhard et al., 2016), nocodazole stimulation led to a GEF-H1-dependent increase in RhoA activity in the cell periphery (see images in Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and citation to Reinhard et al., 2016.

claim: At the Golgi, RhoA activity increases steadily and reaches a plateau 10 min after nocodazole treatment in control cells.
source: At the Golgi, RhoA activity increased steadily and reached a plateau 10 min after nocodazole treatment in control cells.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the FRET imaging experiments.

claim: In GEF-H1 depleted cells, no increase in RhoA activity at the cell periphery and the Golgi is observed after nocodazole treatment.
source: In GEF-H1 depleted cells, however, no increase in RhoA activity at the cell periphery and the Golgi was observed (see images and graph in Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: mDia1 mediates RhoA-induced Golgi fragmentation.
source: For example, mDia1 was reported to mediate RhoA-induced Golgi fragmentation (Zilberman et al., 2011), however, in our experimental system, depletion of mDia1 did not affect RhoA-mediated PKD activation at Golgi membranes (Figure 3A, B and C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zilberman et al., 2011.

claim: Depletion of mDia1 does not affect RhoA-mediated PKD activation at Golgi membranes.
source: For example, mDia1 was reported to mediate RhoA-induced Golgi fragmentation (Zilberman et al., 2011), however, in our experimental system, depletion of mDia1 did not affect RhoA-mediated PKD activation at Golgi membranes (Figure 3A, B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B and C.

claim: ROCK1 and 2 mediate cell contractility downstream of nocodazole-induced Rho activation.
source: The Rho effector kinases ROCK1 and 2 were shown to mediate cell contractility downstream of nocodazole-induced Rho activation (Chang et al., 2008) and expression of constitutive active ROCK1 induced Golgi fragmentation (Orlando and Pittman, 2006), but neither the single, nor the combined depletion of ROCK1 and ROCK2 affected Golgi-associated PKD activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2008.

claim: Expression of constitutive active ROCK1 induces Golgi fragmentation.
source: The Rho effector kinases ROCK1 and 2 were shown to mediate cell contractility downstream of nocodazole-induced Rho activation (Chang et al., 2008) and expression of constitutive active ROCK1 induced Golgi fragmentation (Orlando and Pittman, 2006), but neither the single, nor the combined depletion of ROCK1 and ROCK2 affected Golgi-associated PKD activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Orlando and Pittman, 2006.

claim: Neither the single, nor the combined depletion of ROCK1 and ROCK2 affects Golgi-associated PKD activity.
source: The Rho effector kinases ROCK1 and 2 were shown to mediate cell contractility downstream of nocodazole-induced Rho activation (Chang et al., 2008) and expression of constitutive active ROCK1 induced Golgi fragmentation (Orlando and Pittman, 2006), but neither the single, nor the combined depletion of ROCK1 and ROCK2 affected Golgi-associated PKD activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pharmacological ROCK inhibition by H1152 fails to block RhoA Q63L-induced PKD activation.
source: Pharmacological ROCK inhibition by H1152 also failed to block RhoA Q63L-induced PKD activation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PLCε is a Rho effector protein found to localize to the Golgi complex in cardiac myocytes.
source: PLCε is a Rho effector protein found to localize to the Golgi complex in cardiac myocytes (Zhang et al., 2013) where it hydrolyzes PtdIns(4)P resulting in the production of DAG.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: PLCε hydrolyzes PtdIns(4)P resulting in the production of DAG.
source: PLCε is a Rho effector protein found to localize to the Golgi complex in cardiac myocytes (Zhang et al., 2013) where it hydrolyzes PtdIns(4)P resulting in the production of DAG.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: Depletion of PLCε significantly reduces RhoA-mediated PKD activation at the TGN.
source: Indeed, depletion of PLCε using independent siRNAs significantly reduced RhoA-mediated PKD activation at the TGN (Figures 3A and B and C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A, B, C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In cells depleted of PLCε, nocodazole treatment no longer results in PKD activation.
source: Furthermore, in cells depleted of PLCε, nocodazole treatment no longer resulted in the PKD activation seen in the control cells (Figure 3D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), confirming that PLCε is downstream of RhoA in PKD activation at Golgi membranes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: PLCε is downstream of RhoA in PKD activation at Golgi membranes.
source: Furthermore, in cells depleted of PLCε, nocodazole treatment no longer resulted in the PKD activation seen in the control cells (Figure 3D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), confirming that PLCε is downstream of RhoA in PKD activation at Golgi membranes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The loss of PLCε diminishes GEF-H1 C53R-mediated PKD activation.
source: In control cells, GEF-H1 C53R potently activated PKD whereas the loss of PLCε diminished the GEF-H1 C53R-mediated PKD activation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In cells depleted of PLCε, the amount of PKD1kd at Golgi membranes is reduced compared to control cells.
source: Quantification revealed that in cells depleted of PLCε, the amount of PKD1kd at Golgi membranes was reduced compared to control cells (Figure 4A, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The loss of PLCε decreases DAG at Golgi membranes.
source: Quantification revealed that in cells depleted of PLCε, the amount of PKD1kd at Golgi membranes was reduced compared to control cells (Figure 4A, bottom). This suggests that the loss of PLCε decreases DAG at and thus PKD localization to Golgi membranes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PKD1kd (a DAG sensor) localization to Golgi is reduced upon PLCε depletion.

claim: PLCε depletion leads to a modest but significant reduction in basal PKD activity at TGN membranes compared to control cells.
source: Indeed, quantitative measurement of G-PKDrep phosphorylation revealed that PLCε depletion led to a modest but significant reduction in PKD activity at TGN membranes compared to control cells (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: PLCε is involved in the regulation of both basal PKD activity and nocodazole-induced PKD activation at Golgi membranes.
source: Thus, PLCε is involved in the regulation of both, basal PKD activity and nocodazole-induced PKD activation at Golgi membranes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: In astrocytes, thrombin activates PKD downstream of PLCε.
source: Notably, in astrocytes, thrombin activates PKD downstream of PLCε (Dusaban et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dusaban et al., 2013.

claim: Activation of PAR2 through trypsin induces PKD activity at the Golgi complex.
source: Moreover, activation of PAR2 through trypsin induced PKD activity at the Golgi complex (Jensen et al., 2016), raising the question whether PAR signaling has a physiological function in connecting the plasma membrane with the Golgi complex through GEF-H1.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jensen et al., 2016.

claim: Short trypsin stimulation strongly activates PKD as shown by activation loop phosphorylation of the kinase.
source: Indeed, short trypsin stimulation strongly activated PKD as shown by activation loop phosphorylation of the kinase (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Trypsin treatment significantly activates PKD at the Golgi complex in control cells.
source: Our results clearly show that trypsin treatment significantly activated PKD at the Golgi complex in control cells (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: In cells depleted of GEF-H1, PLCε or PKD2/3, trypsin-mediated PKD activation is diminished compared to control cells.
source: However, in cells depleted of GEF-H1, PLCε or PKD2/3, trypsin-mediated PKD activation was diminished compared to control cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Short thrombin stimulation leads to strong phosphorylation of G-PKDrep which is fully blocked by treatment with the pan-PKD inhibitor CRT0066101.
source: Furthermore, short thrombin stimulation also led to strong phosphorylation of G-PKDrep which was fully blocked by treatment with the pan-PKD inhibitor CRT0066101 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) placing PARs upstream of a GEF-H1-PKD signaling pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: PARs are upstream of a GEF-H1-PKD signaling pathway.
source: Furthermore, short thrombin stimulation also led to strong phosphorylation of G-PKDrep which was fully blocked by treatment with the pan-PKD inhibitor CRT0066101 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) placing PARs upstream of a GEF-H1-PKD signaling pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Deleted in Liver Cancer 3 (DLC3) is a RhoGAP protein with specificity for RhoA.
source: Recently, we identified Deleted in Liver Cancer 3 (DLC3), a RhoGAP protein with specificity for RhoA (Holeiter et al., 2012) to control RhoA-GTP levels at Golgi membranes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holeiter et al., 2012.

claim: Depletion of DLC3 in HeLa cells significantly increases basal RhoA activity at the Golgi compartment resulting in fragmentation of the Golgi complex.
source: Depletion of DLC3 in HeLa cells significantly increased basal RhoA activity at this compartment resulting in fragmentation of the Golgi complex (Braun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Braun et al., 2015.

claim: Depletion of DLC3 results in a significant increase in PKD activity at the TGN.
source: To address whether DLC3 could be a counterplayer of GEF-H1 in PKD activation at the Golgi complex, we depleted DLC3 in HeLa cells and analyzed PKD activity at the TGN using the G-PKDrep phosphorylation as a read out (Figure 5A). Importantly, we detected a significant increase in PKD activity when DLC3 was absent (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Depletion of GEF-H1 or PLCε rescues the PKD activation induced by DLC3 depletion.
source: If DLC3 and GEF-H1 control the same RhoA pool, depletion of GEF-H1 or the Rho effector PLCε should rescue the PKD activation induced by DLC3 depletion. Indeed, when both proteins, DLC3 plus GEF-H1 or DLC3 plus PLCε were depleted, the significant increase in PKD activity as observed in DLC3-depleted cells was fully rescued (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: GEF-H1, Rho and PLCε are in a linear signaling pathway that links the microtubule network with PKD activity at the TGN and is counterbalanced by DLC3.
source: Our results thus indicate that GEF-H1, Rho and PLCε are in a linear signaling pathway that links the microtubule network with PKD activity at the TGN and is counterbalanced by DLC3.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Nocodazole treatment or expression of active RhoA recruits Rab8 to Golgi membranes.
source: A previous report showed that nocodazole treatment or expression of active RhoA recruits Rab8 to Golgi membranes (Hattula et al., 2006), prompting us to investigate whether this is regulated by PKD.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hattula et al., 2006.

claim: In HeLa cells expressing PKD1-GFP, Rab8 co-localizes with p230 and PKD1-GFP at trans-Golgi membranes.
source: In HeLa cells expressing PKD1-GFP, Rab8 co-localized with p230 and PKD1-GFP at trans-Golgi membranes whereas in cells without ectopic PKD1-GFP expression Rab8 was found on tubular and/or vesicular structures, which did not show an overlap with the trans-Golgi marker p230 (Figure 6A, top panel, histograms).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In cells without ectopic PKD1-GFP expression, Rab8 is found on tubular and/or vesicular structures, which do not show an overlap with the trans-Golgi marker p230.
source: In HeLa cells expressing PKD1-GFP, Rab8 co-localized with p230 and PKD1-GFP at trans-Golgi membranes whereas in cells without ectopic PKD1-GFP expression Rab8 was found on tubular and/or vesicular structures, which did not show an overlap with the trans-Golgi marker p230 (Figure 6A, top panel, histograms).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Rab6 is strongly enriched at the TGN, indicated by co-localization with p230 and PKD1-GFP.
source: Rab6 was strongly enriched at the TGN, indicated by the co-localization with p230 and PKD1-GFP, however, the localization of Rab6 at trans-Golgi membranes was independent of PKD1-GFP expression (Figure 6A, bottom panel, and histogram).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The localization of Rab6 at trans-Golgi membranes is independent of PKD1-GFP expression.
source: Rab6 was strongly enriched at the TGN, indicated by the co-localization with p230 and PKD1-GFP, however, the localization of Rab6 at trans-Golgi membranes was independent of PKD1-GFP expression (Figure 6A, bottom panel, and histogram).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ectopic expression of PKD1-GFP or PKD2-GFP significantly increases the Golgi localization of Rab8.
source: Our observations were confirmed by a quantitative object-based co-localization analysis using CellProfiler software (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), which clearly showed that ectopic expression of PKD1-GFP or PKD2-GFP significantly increased the Golgi localization of Rab8, whereas in GFP vector transfected cells Rab8 localization remained unchanged (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In GFP vector transfected cells, Rab8 localization remains unchanged.
source: Our observations were confirmed by a quantitative object-based co-localization analysis using CellProfiler software (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), which clearly showed that ectopic expression of PKD1-GFP or PKD2-GFP significantly increased the Golgi localization of Rab8, whereas in GFP vector transfected cells Rab8 localization remained unchanged (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: PKD is upstream of Rab8 recruitment to Golgi membranes.
source: Our results thus position PKD upstream of Rab8 recruitment to Golgi membranes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Rab6 is connected to a FA-directed exocytosis pathway.
source: Recently, Rab6 was connected to a FA-directed exocytosis pathway.
evidence: This is stated as recent knowledge.

claim: The docking and fusion of Rab6 vesicles within the plasma membrane occurs preferentially near FAs.
source: The docking and fusion of Rab6 vesicles within the plasma membrane occurred preferentially near FAs (Stehbens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stehbens et al., 2014.

claim: Loss of GEF-H1, PLCε, or PKD2/PKD3 significantly decreases the number of Rab6A-positive vesicles arriving at FAs.
source: Loss of GEF-H1, PLCε, or PKD2/PKD3, however, significantly decreased the number of Rab6A-positive vesicles arriving at FAs, with cells depleted of the two PKD isoforms showing the strongest effect (Figure 7A and C, Figure 7—Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and C.

claim: Cells depleted of PKD2 and PKD3 show the strongest effect in reducing Rab6A-positive vesicles arriving at FAs.
source: Loss of GEF-H1, PLCε, or PKD2/PKD3, however, significantly decreased the number of Rab6A-positive vesicles arriving at FAs, with cells depleted of the two PKD isoforms showing the strongest effect (Figure 7A and C, Figure 7—Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and C.

claim: The total number of FAs per cell is not affected by the loss of GEF-H1, PLCε, or PKD2/PKD3.
source: Of note, the total number of FAs per cell was not affected by the loss of any of the proteins (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The depletion of GEF-H1 results in an upregulation of PLCε mRNA levels.
source: Interestingly, the depletion of GEF-H1 resulted in an upregulation of PLCε mRNA levels supporting the molecular connection of the two proteins (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Depletion of DLC3 slightly decreases the number of vesicles arriving at FAs compared to control cells.
source: Notably, depletion of DLC3 slightly decreased the number of vesicles arriving at FAs compared to control cells although PKD activity was increased under these conditions (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: DLC3 depletion induces the fragmentation of the Golgi complex.
source: However, as DLC3 depletion induced the fragmentation of the Golgi complex (see Figure 5A and [Braun et al., 2015]) it is likely that the polarized delivery of Rab6 vesicles to FAs is negatively affected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and citation to Braun et al., 2015.

claim: Rho levels at the Golgi complex have to be tightly regulated to ensure proper vesicular trafficking.
source: This also supports the hypothesis that Rho levels at the Golgi complex have to be tightly regulated to ensure proper vesicular trafficking.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both loss and hyperactivation of Rho disrupt trafficking.

claim: Thrombin stimulation significantly increases the number of Rab6 vesicles arriving at FAs in control but not in PKD2/3 depleted cells.
source: Our data clearly show that thrombin stimulation significantly increased the number of Rab6 vesicles arriving at FAs in control but not in PKD2/3 depleted cells (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Activation of PARs induces PKD-dependent localized exocytosis.
source: We thus demonstrate that activation of PARs induces PKD-dependent localized exocytosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: In PLCε-depleted cells, microtubule plus ends contact FAs as efficiently as in control cells.
source: As shown by the kymographs, in PLCε-depleted cells microtubule plus ends contacted FAs as efficiently as in control cells, proving that the loss of the Rho effector PLCε does not interfere with the microtubule-FA interaction per se (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The loss of PLCε does not interfere with the microtubule-FA interaction per se.
source: As shown by the kymographs, in PLCε-depleted cells microtubule plus ends contacted FAs as efficiently as in control cells, proving that the loss of the Rho effector PLCε does not interfere with the microtubule-FA interaction per se (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Perturbations of the GEF-H1/Rho/PLCε/PKD signaling axis affect Rab6 vesicles already at the level of the TGN.
source: We thus conclude that perturbations of the GEF-H1/Rho/PLCε/PKD signaling axis affect Rab6 vesicles already at the level of the TGN.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: TNFα is transported in Rab6 vesicles from the TGN to the plasma membrane.
source: Since TNFα was shown to be transported in Rab6 vesicles from the TGN to the plasma membrane ([Micaroni et al., 2013] and Figure 8A) and is exocytosed at FAs (personal correspondence F. Perez (Institute Curie, Paris) November, 2017), we studied whether TNFα secretion is controlled by the GEF-H1-dependent Rho signaling network.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Micaroni et al., 2013 and experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: TNFα is exocytosed at FAs.
source: Since TNFα was shown to be transported in Rab6 vesicles from the TGN to the plasma membrane ([Micaroni et al., 2013] and Figure 8A) and is exocytosed at FAs (personal correspondence F. Perez (Institute Curie, Paris) November, 2017), we studied whether TNFα secretion is controlled by the GEF-H1-dependent Rho signaling network.
evidence: This is supported by personal correspondence with F. Perez.

claim: TNFα-SBP-mCherry clearly leaves the Golgi and reaches the plasma membrane after biotin addition in control cells.
source: While TNFα-SBP-mCherry clearly left the Golgi and reached the plasma membrane after biotin addition in control cells, GEF-H1, PLCε, and PKD2/3 knockdown caused a substantial block in transport of TNFα-SBP-mCherry from the TGN to the plasma membrane (Figure 8C and D, Figure 8—Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: GEF-H1, PLCε, and PKD2/3 knockdown causes a substantial block in transport of TNFα-SBP-mCherry from the TGN to the plasma membrane.
source: While TNFα-SBP-mCherry clearly left the Golgi and reached the plasma membrane after biotin addition in control cells, GEF-H1, PLCε, and PKD2/3 knockdown caused a substantial block in transport of TNFα-SBP-mCherry from the TGN to the plasma membrane (Figure 8C and D, Figure 8—Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: No changes in the trafficking of TNFα between the ER and the Golgi complex were observed upon GEF-H1, PLCε, or PKD2/3 knockdown.
source: Notably, we could not observe any changes in the trafficking of TNFα between the ER and the Golgi complex (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: Rho-controlled PKD activation at the TGN induces the fission of Rab6-vesicles containing cargo for targeted exocytosis at FAs.
source: These data clearly show that Rho-controlled PKD activation at the TGN induces the fission of Rab6-vesicles containing cargo for targeted exocytosis at FAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The study identifies a Rho-dependent signaling network connecting microtubules with PKD-dependent vesicle fission at the TGN.
source: Here we identify a Rho-dependent signaling network connecting microtubules with PKD-dependent vesicle fission at the TGN.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: GEF-H1, when released from microtubules, enhances cellular RhoA activity, which in turn promotes PKD activation at the TGN through the Rho effector PLCε, ultimately leading to the fission of Rab6-positive vesicles that move towards FAs.
source: Specifically, we demonstrate that GEF-H1, when released from microtubules, enhances cellular RhoA activity, which in turn promotes PKD activation at the TGN through the Rho effector PLCε, ultimately leading to the fission of Rab6-positive vesicles that move towards FAs.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study summarizing the signaling pathway.

claim: GEF-H1 is crucial for the coupling of microtubule dynamics to Rho GTPase activation in several biological situations such as cell polarization and motility and cell cycle regulation.
source: The RhoGEF GEF-H1 is crucial for the coupling of microtubule dynamics to Rho GTPase activation in several biological situations such as cell polarization and motility and cell cycle regulation (reviewed in [Birkenfeld et al., 2008]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Birkenfeld et al., 2008.

claim: GEF-H1 is a well-known activator of RhoA but it can also act as a GEF for RhoB.
source: GEF-H1 is a well-known activator of RhoA but it can also act as a GEF for RhoB (Arnette et al., 2016; Vega et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arnette et al., 2016 and Vega et al., 2012.

claim: Release and activation of GEF-H1 can be achieved by disrupting polymerized microtubules through pharmacological compounds or, independent of microtubule disassembly, through GPCR signaling.
source: Release and activation of GEF-H1 can be achieved by disrupting polymerized microtubules through pharmacological compounds or, independent of microtubule disassembly, through GPCR signaling (Meiri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meiri et al., 2014.

claim: Both nocodazole treatment and trypsin or thrombin-induced GPCR stimulation initiate a Rho signaling cascade leading to PKD activation and the fission of vesicles at TGN membranes.
source: Here we show that both modes of GEF-H1 activation, nocodazole treatment and trypsin or thrombin-induced GPCR stimulation, initiate a Rho signaling cascade leading to PKD activation and the fission of vesicles at TGN membranes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: GEF-H1 interacts with the exocyst component Sec5 leading to local RhoA activation thereby promoting exocyst assembly and exocytosis.
source: Bokoch and co-workers showed that GEF-H1 interacts with the exocyst component Sec5 leading to local RhoA activation thereby promoting exocyst assembly and exocytosis (Pathak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pathak et al., 2012.

claim: The targeted trafficking of c-Src–associated endosomes to the cell periphery depends on the GEF-H1-mediated activation of endosomal RhoB.
source: Additionally, the targeted trafficking of c-Src–associated endosomes to the cell periphery was reported to depend on the GEF-H1-mediated activation of endosomal RhoB (Arnette et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arnette et al., 2016.

claim: The subcellular localization of the microtubule-regulated GEF-H1 determines the spatio-temporal activation of specific Rho pools and Rho isoforms.
source: It is thus evident that the subcellular localization of the microtubule-regulated GEF-H1 determines the spatio-temporal activation of specific Rho pools and Rho isoforms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited literature.

claim: The junctional adaptor cingulin recruits GEF-H1 to tight junctions thereby inactivating its GEF activity and inhibiting Rho signaling.
source: For example, the junctional adaptor cingulin recruits GEF-H1 to tight junctions thereby inactivating its GEF activity and inhibiting Rho signaling (Aijaz et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aijaz et al., 2005.

claim: The interaction of GEF-H1 with Sec5 promotes RhoA activation at the exocyst complex.
source: By contrast, the interaction of GEF-H1 with Sec5 promotes RhoA activation at the exocyst complex (Pathak et al., 2012) and is important for GEF-H1 localization to FAs (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pathak et al., 2012.

claim: The interaction of GEF-H1 with Sec5 is important for GEF-H1 localization to FAs.
source: By contrast, the interaction of GEF-H1 with Sec5 promotes RhoA activation at the exocyst complex (Pathak et al., 2012) and is important for GEF-H1 localization to FAs (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Plasma membrane associated active RhoA recruits GEF-H1 thereby promoting a self-amplification loop.
source: Recently, plasma membrane associated active RhoA was demonstrated to recruit GEF-H1 thereby promoting a self-amplification loop.
evidence: This is stated as recent knowledge.

claim: Active RhoA inhibits itself by the local recruitment of the actomyosin-associated RhoGAP Myo9b.
source: At the same time, active RhoA was also shown to inhibit itself by the local recruitment of the actomyosin-associated RhoGAP Myo9b (Graessl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Graessl et al., 2017.

claim: A similar autoregulatory loop involving GEF-H1, Rho and the RhoGAP DLC3 might drive the self-limiting fission of exocytic vesicles at the TGN.
source: A similar autoregulatory loop involving GEF-H1, Rho and the RhoGAP DLC3 might drive the self-limiting fission of exocytic vesicles at the TGN.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the analogy with the plasma membrane system.

claim: Previous reports demonstrated GEF-H1 localization to Golgi membranes.
source: Although previous reports demonstrated GEF-H1 localization to Golgi membranes (Birkenfeld et al., 2007; Callow et al., 2005), we were not able to detect endogenous or ectopically expressed GEF-H1 at the TGN.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Birkenfeld et al., 2007 and Callow et al., 2005.

claim: The authors were not able to detect endogenous or ectopically expressed GEF-H1 at the TGN.
source: Although previous reports demonstrated GEF-H1 localization to Golgi membranes (Birkenfeld et al., 2007; Callow et al., 2005), we were not able to detect endogenous or ectopically expressed GEF-H1 at the TGN.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: Hyperactivation of Rho has been linked to Golgi complex fragmentation.
source: Hyperactivation of Rho has been linked to Golgi complex fragmentation (Cole et al., 1996; Zilberman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cole et al., 1996 and Zilberman et al., 2011.

claim: Zilberman and colleagues identified the Rho effector mDia1 to be responsible for the RhoA-induced Golgi fragmentation.
source: Zilberman and colleagues identified the Rho effector mDia1 to be responsible for the RhoA-induced Golgi fragmentation (Zilberman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zilberman et al., 2011.

claim: The inhibition or loss of PKD delays nocodazole-induced Golgi fragmentation.
source: Although the inhibition or loss of PKD delayed nocodazole-induced Golgi fragmentation (Fuchs et al., 2009), we show here that mDia1 is not responsible for PKD activation downstream of Rho.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fuchs et al., 2009.

claim: mDia1 is not responsible for PKD activation downstream of Rho.
source: Although the inhibition or loss of PKD delayed nocodazole-induced Golgi fragmentation (Fuchs et al., 2009), we show here that mDia1 is not responsible for PKD activation downstream of Rho.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: In hippocampal neurons, PKD1 activation at the Golgi occurs via a RhoA/ROCK signaling pathway and is required for the formation of Golgi outposts.
source: In hippocampal neurons, PKD1 activation at the Golgi occurs via a RhoA/ROCK signaling pathway and is required for the formation of Golgi outposts (Quassollo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Quassollo et al., 2015.

claim: In HeLa cells ROCK1 and 2 are dispensable for RhoA-mediated PKD activation.
source: In HeLa cells ROCK1 and 2 were dispensable for RhoA-mediated PKD activation, instead, we identified PLCε as the key Rho effector.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: PLCε is the key Rho effector for PKD activation in HeLa cells.
source: In HeLa cells ROCK1 and 2 were dispensable for RhoA-mediated PKD activation, instead, we identified PLCε as the key Rho effector.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Within the PI-PLC family, PLCε has an outstanding role because it is an effector of the small GTPases Rho and Ras and further acts as a GEF protein for Rap1.
source: Within the PI-PLC family, PLCε has an outstanding role because it is an effector of the small GTPases Rho and Ras and further acts as a GEF protein for Rap1 (Dusaban and Brown, 2015; Wing et al., 2003a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dusaban and Brown, 2015 and Wing et al., 2003a.

claim: Stimulated by the direct binding to RhoA, RhoB, or RhoC, PLCε hydrolyzes PtdIns(4,5)P2 to generate DAG and IP3.
source: Stimulated by the direct binding to RhoA, RhoB, or RhoC, PLCε hydrolyzes PtdIns(4,5)P2 to generate DAG and IP3 (Wing et al., 2003b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wing et al., 2003b.

claim: In cardiac myocytes PLCε is localized to a perinuclear compartment through binding to a muscle-specific A-kinase anchoring protein β (mAKAPβ).
source: In cardiac myocytes PLCε is localized to a perinuclear compartment through binding to a muscle-specific A-kinase anchoring protein β (mAKAPβ) (Zhang et al., 2011, 2013) and hydrolyzes PtdIns(4)P to generate DAG and IP2 (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2011, 2013.

claim: The PLCε/DAG-activated PKD translocates to the nucleus and induces the transcription of hypertrophic genes in cardiac myocytes.
source: Subsequently, the PLCε/DAG-activated PKD translocates to the nucleus and induces the transcription of hypertrophic genes (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: PLCε mediates sustained signaling by driving a positive feedback loop through the small GTPase Rap1.
source: Interestingly, PLCε mediates sustained signaling by driving a positive feedback loop through the small GTPase Rap1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Rap1 recruits PLCε to the Golgi complex, and PLCε in turn activates Rap1, which strengthens the PLCε association with Golgi membranes thereby maintaining local DAG levels.
source: Smrcka and colleagues suggested a model in which Rap1 recruits PLCε to the Golgi complex. PLCε in turn activates Rap1, which strengthens the PLCε association with Golgi membranes thereby maintaining local DAG levels (Smrcka et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smrcka et al., 2012.

claim: Gβγ signaling at the Golgi complex triggers PLCε activation in cardiac myocytes.
source: Intriguingly, Gβγ signaling at the Golgi complex triggered PLCε activation in cardiac myocytes (Zhang et al., 2013), however, so far this has not been connected to Rho and/or PKD-dependent vesicle fission at this compartment.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: The DAG pool produced by PLCε is required for basal and GPCR-induced PKD activity at the TGN.
source: Based on our findings we conclude that the DAG pool produced by PLCε is also required for basal and GPCR-induced PKD activity at the TGN, thereby linking GEF-H1-controlled Rho activity with Golgi function and transport.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: DLC3 is the only RhoGAP protein that has been associated with Golgi membranes.
source: Thus far, DLC3 is the only RhoGAP protein that has been associated with Golgi membranes.
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge.

claim: Depletion of DLC3 results in Golgi fragmentation, most likely due to enhanced local Rho activity.
source: Depletion of DLC3 resulted in Golgi fragmentation, most likely due to enhanced local Rho activity (Braun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Braun et al., 2015.

claim: DLC3 counteracts GEF-H1-mediated Rho and consequently PKD activation at TGN membranes.
source: We now provide evidence that DLC3 counteracts GEF-H1-mediated Rho and consequently PKD activation at TGN membranes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: DLC3 is required for the integrity of the Rab8 compartment.
source: Furthermore, DLC3 is required for the integrity of the Rab8 compartment (Braun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Braun et al., 2015.

claim: Loss of DLC3 and therefore increased Rho activity impairs the tubule-like distribution of Rab8 and converts it to a vesicular phenotype with enhanced perinuclear localization.
source: Loss of DLC3 and therefore increased Rho activity impaired the tubule-like distribution of Rab8 and converted it to a vesicular phenotype with enhanced perinuclear localization.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: RhoA G14V expression or nocodazole treatment redistributes Rab8 to the perinuclear region.
source: This is consistent with observations by Hattula et al. showing that RhoA G14V expression or nocodazole treatment redistributed Rab8 to the perinuclear region.
evidence: This is stated as consistent with prior observations.

claim: Expression of active PKD1 or PKD2 induces a similar Rab8 phenotype as DLC3 depletion.
source: Remarkably, we observed a similar Rab8 phenotype upon expression of active PKD1 or PKD2 demonstrating that PKD is upstream of Rab8 localization.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: PKD is upstream of Rab8 localization.
source: Remarkably, we observed a similar Rab8 phenotype upon expression of active PKD1 or PKD2 demonstrating that PKD is upstream of Rab8 localization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Rab6 and Rab8 localize to the same Golgi-derived exocytic carriers, with Rab6 controlling Rab8 localization.
source: Rab6 and Rab8 localize to the same Golgi-derived exocytic carriers, with Rab6 controlling Rab8 localization (Grigoriev et al., 2007; Grigoriev et al., 2011; Jones et al., 1993; Wakana et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grigoriev et al., 2007; Grigoriev et al., 2011; Jones et al., 1993; Wakana et al., 2012.

claim: PKD is not only required for the fission of Rab6/Rab8 carriers but also responsible for the proper assembly of Rab8 at the TGN.
source: We thus hypothesize that PKD is not only required for the fission of these carriers but also responsible for the proper assembly of Rab8 at the TGN.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Rab6 acts on TNFα trafficking at the level of TGN exit and is required for the efficient post-Golgi transport of TNFα in inflammatory macrophages.
source: Our data are thus in line with a previous study showing that Rab6 acts on TNFα trafficking at the level of TGN exit and is required for the efficient post-Golgi transport of TNFα in inflammatory macrophages (Micaroni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Micaroni et al., 2013.

claim: In inflammatory macrophages and monocytes, TNFα secretion is induced by lipopolysaccharides.
source: In inflammatory macrophages and monocytes, TNFα secretion is induced by lipopolysaccharides (Micaroni et al., 2013) and further augmented by thrombin (Hoffman and Cooper, 1995), respectively, supporting our data that connect GPCR signaling with PKD activation at the TGN.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Micaroni et al., 2013.

claim: TNFα secretion is augmented by thrombin in monocytes.
source: In inflammatory macrophages and monocytes, TNFα secretion is induced by lipopolysaccharides (Micaroni et al., 2013) and further augmented by thrombin (Hoffman and Cooper, 1995), respectively, supporting our data that connect GPCR signaling with PKD activation at the TGN.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hoffman and Cooper, 1995.

claim: Rab6-positive vesicles have been associated with the exocytosis of MT1-MMP near FAs.
source: Likewise, Rab6-positive vesicles have been associated with the exocytosis of MT1-MMP near FAs (Stehbens et al., 2014) and a recent report showed for the first time the targeted delivery of integrin-rich vesicles to FAs (Huet-Calderwood et al., 2017) establishing these structures as cellular hot spots of secretion.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stehbens et al., 2014.

claim: A recent report showed the targeted delivery of integrin-rich vesicles to FAs.
source: Likewise, Rab6-positive vesicles have been associated with the exocytosis of MT1-MMP near FAs (Stehbens et al., 2014) and a recent report showed for the first time the targeted delivery of integrin-rich vesicles to FAs (Huet-Calderwood et al., 2017) establishing these structures as cellular hot spots of secretion.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huet-Calderwood et al., 2017.

claim: Focal adhesions are cellular hot spots of secretion.
source: Likewise, Rab6-positive vesicles have been associated with the exocytosis of MT1-MMP near FAs (Stehbens et al., 2014) and a recent report showed for the first time the targeted delivery of integrin-rich vesicles to FAs (Huet-Calderwood et al., 2017) establishing these structures as cellular hot spots of secretion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited literature.

claim: Constitutively active RhoA augments the production of Rab6-positive vesicles.
source: Constitutively active RhoA was reported to augment the production of Rab6-positive vesicles (Zilberman et al., 2011) and Rab6-positive vesicles were shown to move along microtubules targeting FAs, thereby contributing to FA turnover during directed cell migration (Stehbens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zilberman et al., 2011.

claim: Rab6-positive vesicles move along microtubules targeting FAs, thereby contributing to FA turnover during directed cell migration.
source: Constitutively active RhoA was reported to augment the production of Rab6-positive vesicles (Zilberman et al., 2011) and Rab6-positive vesicles were shown to move along microtubules targeting FAs, thereby contributing to FA turnover during directed cell migration (Stehbens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stehbens et al., 2014.

claim: GEF-H1, PLCε, or PKD are required for the formation and transport of Rab6-positive vesicles to FAs.
source: We show here that GEF-H1, PLCε, or PKD are required for the formation and transport of these vesicles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: The study provides an explanation for the previously reported effects of GEF-H1 loss on cell spreading and FA turnover.
source: Our results thus provide an explanation for the previously reported effects of GEF-H1 loss on cell spreading and FA turnover (Nalbant et al., 2009; Vega et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: Extracellular matrix stiffness destabilizes microtubules, releasing GEF-H1, which is required for the invasion of breast cancer cells through 3D matrices.
source: Interestingly, extracellular matrix stiffness was found to destabilize microtubules, releasing GEF-H1, which was required for the invasion of breast cancer cells through 3D matrices (Heck et al., 2012).

claim: Microtubules, through Rho-mediated activation of Golgi-localized PKD, may sense extracellular matrix density to coordinate Golgi secretory function with the increased demand for factors such as proteases or cytokines required for ECM remodeling during invasive 3D migration.
